title: Granitos
subtitle: Several straight stitches into the same two holes to build a small padded seed or petal
excerpt: Granitos is a tiny padded shape made by working multiple straight stitches between the same two entry and exit holes, fanning the thread slightly with each stitch to build up a rounded, seed-like form. It needs no separate padding and no special tools. The result is a small raised bead of thread that reads as a seed, berry, or narrow petal depending on the length and thread used.
sourceNotes: Granitos (Spanish: small grains) appears in Iberian and Latin American needlework traditions. Contemporary surface embroidery documentation; the self-padding principle of stacking threads in the same two holes is consistent with padded straight stitch technique described in Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

content.text: Granitos means small grains in Spanish, and that describes the finished shape exactly. Three to five straight stitches are worked in and out of the same pair of holes, with each pass laid beside the last. Because the holes stay fixed, the threads naturally bow and press against each other, creating a small rounded mound without any separate padding underneath. The shape can be made rounder or more oval by the number of stitches and by the degree to which you fan them at the centre.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton 2 to 4 strands; more strands build a plumper shape faster

content.text: Bring the thread up at point (A) and take it down at point (B). The distance between (A) and (B) sets the length of the granitos. Keep these first holes small and precise.

Bring the thread up at (A) again, as close to the first exit as possible without splitting the fabric. Take it down at (B) again in the same way. Lay this second stitch slightly to one side of the first so they lie beside each other rather than on top.

Work a third stitch from (A) to (B), this time on the opposite side of the first stitch. The three stitches now fan slightly at the centre, pressing against each other and lifting into a rounded shape.
Add a fourth or fifth stitch from (A) to (B) if a rounder, more padded shape is needed. Each stitch fans a little further than the last. Fasten off at the back when the shape is full and even.

items.symptom: The shape is flat rather than rounded
items.cause: All stitches were laid exactly on top of each other rather than fanning slightly at the centre.
items.fix: On each pass, move the needle just a fraction sideways when coming up at (A) so successive stitches fan outward at the midpoint.

items.symptom: The holes at (A) and (B) are visible and untidy
items.cause: The needle was inserted too far from the previous hole, enlarging the entry points.
items.fix: Always bring the needle up and down into the same two holes. Use the needle tip to ease thread gently rather than pulling hard through a new hole.

items.symptom: The granitos looks elongated rather than seed-shaped
items.cause: Too few stitches were used for the thread weight, or the fanning was not wide enough.
items.fix: Add one or two more stitches and fan them to cover the full width at the centre. A round granitos typically needs at least three to four passes.
